certainty_reasoning: Cook states plainly that Ives shared his bed with Harold Holt ('Cubby') at the Albany, which is more explicit than the household-membership evidence behind the Bloodworth record. It stays 'alleged' on the single-source rule: Cook (2003) is the only work read that attests it, and bed-sharing in a shared bachelor household is not by itself a statement of sexual relations. Corroboration: Cook returns to this household at much greater length in Queer Domesticities (2014), where he states that the Adelaide Road relationships 'possibly started sexually' before settling into something platonic, with bed-sharing continuing throughout. Cook's account of the Ives household is drawn from Ives's own 122-volume diary and his endnotes cite it by volume and date; the tier follows whose testimony underlies the claim, not whether our record happens to carry a direct quotation rather than the historian's summary of the same diary.

sources.quote: When Pug and another long term resident Cubby (Charles Gee) were both away he wrote in his diary: 'I feel sad. I love those two, deeply, tenderly [.] Love's quite different from passion [.] to sleep side by side with one's comrade is beyond all worlds beautiful. Not exciting, but oh such a protection and sympathy, of healing to the heart's many wounds'.
sources.context: Cook quoting Ives's diary (vol. 76, 20 January 1921, p. 25, per Cook's endnote 35) on Pug and Cubby being away; the ellipses are Cook's own
sources.supports: Promoted to lead and quote extended by the Q2 quality pass. This is the only passage on this edge in which a participant speaks: Ives's diary, vol. 76, 20 January 1921, as quoted by Cook. The record previously led with Cook's narration and stopped this quotation at 'beyond all worlds beautiful', cutting the clause where Ives says what the bond gave him - 'Not exciting, but oh such a protection and sympathy, of healing to the heart's many wounds'. Ives names love, disclaims passion, and locates the value in comfort; that is the most explicit account of this relationship in his own words that survives in the sources read. The crux of the Cubby identity conflict: Cook 2014 glosses Cubby as 'Charles Gee', where Cook 2003 p. 146 (quoted above in this record) glosses Cubby as 'Harold Holt'. Same author; neither statement carries a source note; the name 'Holt' does not appear anywhere in the 2014 book. Recorded so the conflict is visible in the record itself. Not resolved here - awaits a decision. Also carries Ives's own declaration of love for the two men and his explicit separation of love from passion.
